text: Read the following case and answer the questions mentioned below: Rohan is a senior sales executive at EcoPrint Solutions, a company that sells sustainable printing systems to corporate offices. EcoPrint’s flagship product, GreenEdge X5, uses recycled cartridges and consumes 40% less electricity than conventional printers. The machine costs ₹2.5 lakh per unit, about 25% higher than regular printers. Rohan has secured a meeting with NovaCorp, a mid-sized financial consultancy that prints thousands of pages every week. The procurement head, Meera Sharma, is interested in exploring sustainable alternatives but faces strict cost-cutting directives from management. NovaCorp’s current supplier has offered a lower price and long-term service contract, making Meera hesitant to switch. Rohan must convince Meera that GreenEdge X5 is not just an eco-friendly choice but a financially smart one. Meera, on the other hand wants solid evidence that the product will reduce long-term expenses and align with NovaCorp’s brand image of responsible business practices. How can Rohan design and justify a persuasive sales strategy for GreenEdge X5 by integrating and evaluating the three elements of Aristotle’s persuasion model, credibility, emotion, and logic, to effectively influence Meera’s decision?  &

text: Case - When India’s Chandrayaan-2 mission lost contact with its lander moments before touchdown silence filled the ISRO control room. Years of work, sleepless nights, and national hopes seemed to collapse in a single instant. Scientists sat frozen, their faces lit by the dim glow of monitors. In that heavy silence, ISRO Chairman Dr. K. Sivan rose from his seat. He did not search for someone to blame. Instead he faced his team and said softly, “We did everything we could. This is not a failure—it is a step forward.” His voice carried calm assurance, cutting through the tension in the room. He moved from desk to desk speaking personally to the engineers and young scientists who had worked under him, telling them how proud he was of their dedication. Many were on the verge of tears; he reminded them that no mission is wasted when it teaches something valuable. The next morning, as the world watched, Dr. Sivan took full responsibility before the media, calling the outcome “a learning experience” and emphasizing the team’s achievements in bringing the mission so close to success. He avoided technical blame or excuses, choosing instead to focus on the team’s spirit and resilience. Later, when Prime Minister Modi arrived to encourage the scientists, Dr. Sivan, overwhelmed with emotion, broke down. It was a rare, human moment for a scientist known for his composure. Yet that vulnerability only strengthened his team’s respect for him. They saw a leader who stood with them in failure, protected them in public and guided them back to confidence. In the months that followed, his words became the team’s motivation as they began preparing for the next mission, proof that leadership is not about command, but about compassion and courage in moments of loss.
